Its range spans concrete battlefield victories (as in the accounts in Judges and Samuel) and the more inward or spiritual cry for God's saving help (especially across its 13 occurrences in Psalms). The ancient Greek translators chose σωτηρία — the same word the New Testament uses for 'salvation' — in 19 of their renderings, showing how naturally this Hebrew concept of rescue flowed into later theological language. The word appears almost entirely in poetry and historical narrative, with little use in law or wisdom instruction.
prose.caution: The moderate confidence tier reflects some uncertainty about the precise boundary between its physical-rescue and spiritual-salvation senses, which often overlap and are difficult to separate cleanly in context.

The KJV consistently renders it simply as 'desire,' but the LXX is notably inconsistent — twice using ὀρθῶς ('rightly' or 'correctly') and once ἐπιστροφή ('turning toward'), suggesting ancient translators themselves wrestled with the word's precise force.

The two anomalous LXX renderings as θάλασσα (sea) and ὁρίζω (to bound) likely reflect different Hebrew manuscript traditions in those passages rather than a different sense of the word itself.

It appears most heavily in Genesis (6 times), where it marks the advanced ages of patriarchs — most famously Abraham at age ninety-nine and Sarah at ninety when Isaac was promised. prose.def: Tattenai, a Persian provincial governor who investigated Jewish temple-rebuilding under Darius the Great.
prose.article: Tattenai is a personal name appearing all 4 of its Old Testament occurrences within the single book of Ezra. He was a Persian official — likely the governor of the Trans-Euphrates province — who questioned the Jews' authority to rebuild the Jerusalem temple and wrote to King Darius about it. Notably, when Darius confirmed the Jews' right to build, Tattenai complied fully (Ezra 6:13), making him a minor but historically grounded figure in the post-exilic narrative.
